en: The Supreme Mahāyāna Vajra Great Teaching, the Jewel King Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Grand Master for the Transmission of the Teachings, the Subject Fǎtián, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī in the Āmrapālī Grove.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of six hundred thousand bhikṣus,
among whom were the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa,
the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa, and the Venerable Subhūti.
The Venerable Cunda, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Kapphiṇa,
the Venerable Makhādeva, and the Venerable Upāli.
Venerable Ānanda,
there was a community of bhikṣus numbering six million, such as these,
together with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Their names were the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrama,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaketu.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Padmakuṇḍala, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nityadṛḍhakāya,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnavyūhasāgaraprajñā.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pure Wondrous Sound,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Lamp Radiance,
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Attained Wondrous Sound.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Yathāmanas-prabhāsa; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvalokadhātuprasṛtasiṃhagati;
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalakanakaprabha.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Skillful in Demeanor and Skillful in Conduct;
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Earth-Arising Sustainer of the World King;
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Firm Sound of Celestial Speech.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvadharmavaśavartin,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya,
and six million other such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas were all present together.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance from his mouth;
that light was brilliant and surpassing the sun and moon, and possessed various colors, namely blue.
Yellow, white, red, and green—
there were such countless varieties of colored light that illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds, reaching even as far as the Brahma realm.
Having shone thus, [the light] returned and entered through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda—
He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence,
and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One."
The Tathāgata does not emit light without cause or condition.
For what cause and for what condition has the World-Honored One today emitted this great radiance?
We pray only that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, [will explain].
"Out of great compassion that covers all extensively, please speak for our sake.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"What you have said is not without cause or condition."
Listen attentively, and I shall explain this to you in detail.

Ānanda, there are now immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who have attained the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), up to and including the attainment of the realm of nirvāṇa.
For this reason and by these causes, he emitted this radiance.
While these words were being spoken, there was a devaputra named Indrabhūti,
who led a host of the fourfold army.
Taking various articles of offering, they approached the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, they respectfully made offerings with all those articles,
prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Having formed this thought, "I now wish to hear the most profound Dharma," he again prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms in reverent salutation.
And he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Bhagavat, Great Master of the Three Realms,
and even Father of all sentient beings..."
I am like a small child, foolish and lacking wisdom, and furthermore devoid of skillful means;
I am also like a blind man, full of anger and resentment.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will have compassion for me.
"What skillful means should I employ so that my faculties may attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) with respect to all objects?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the king, saying: "Excellent, excellent! I understand what you have asked."
For the sake of sentient beings in the future age of the Dharma's decay,
desiring to cause them to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*),
the World-Honored One then addressed the Great King, saying:
"I possess four supreme dharmas;
whoever hears them shall certainly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Ānanda heard these words within the great assembly.
He immediately prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, and said:
"World-Honored One, what are called the four kinds of dharmas?
The Buddha replied: "As for the four kinds of dharmas..."
These are what are called the Śrāvaka-yāna and the Pratyekabuddha-yāna;
these two vehicles are capable only of benefiting oneself and not of benefiting others.
Furthermore, there are two other vehicles.
That is to say, the Vaipulya Mahāyāna and the supreme Vajra Mahāyāna;
these are called the four.
At that time, Ānanda asked again:
"What is the nature of this Vajra Mahāyāna?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda,
if there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to the supreme mind of great enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta)..."
This is precisely what is called the nature of the Vajrayāna.
This bodhicitta is able to benefit oneself and further benefit others.
Thus, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices and understands skillful means.
One will be able to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) with respect to the various objects, conditions,
and activities of each of the sense faculties. At that time, King Indrabhūti—
Having heard the World-Honored One speak these four dharmas for Ānanda, he was greatly delighted.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva understand skillful means,
such that they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) regarding the objects, conditions, and activities of each of the sense faculties?
The Buddha said, 'Great King, [it is as follows:]'"
In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable great kalpas ago,
there appeared in the world a Buddha named Pure Radiance Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
That Buddha-world is named Great Sublime Fragrance.
The lifespan of that Tathāgata Pure Radiance of the Sun remains for ninety thousand kalpas.
All sentient beings in that Buddha-world possess sharp and keen wisdom,
and they have all resolved their minds upon great bodhicitta.
At that time, there was a king named Vīryadatta.
With power like that of a Wheel-Turning King leading his fourfold army,
he proceeded with attendants before and behind to the abode of that Buddha,
further offering various kinds of incense and flowers as an oblation to him.
Having extended his offerings, he prostrated, circumambulated, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One:
"How can one cause the faculties, their objects, the focal points, and their activities [to be purified]?"
One shall attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present..."
They all likewise explain this skillful means:
by understanding the respective objects, conditions, and functions of the various faculties,
one is able to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then Vīryadatta again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
The Buddha said, "As for the nature of a bodhisattva..."
These are precisely great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity.
These four dharmas constitute the nature of a bodhisattva;
a bodhisattva delights in practicing these four dharmas.
He is able to cause all sentient beings to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Tathāgata Sun-Pure Radiance (*Sūryaviśuddhaprabha*) looked toward the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas on his left side.
He addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"Vajrapāṇi, you should go to the palace of King Vīradatta and [explain] the Vajra Mahāyāna as the king has asked."
You should, for the sake of the king and all sentient beings according to their various faculties and natures, expound upon the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of skillful means,
so that they may attain the forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Upon hearing the Buddha’s command, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha.
He spoke these words:
"I shall now, in accordance with the holy intent of the Tathāgata, go forth to deliver and liberate them.
At that time, King Vīryadatta heard the Buddha’s words.
He then proceeded before the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
prostrated with his head at [the Bodhisattva’s] feet, and made this request:
"I pray only that the Bodhisattva, in obedience to the Buddha’s command and out of compassion for my sincere devotion, will deign to visit my palace."
Please expound for me the Vajra Mahāyāna,
so that I may attain understanding and realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
and likewise bring great benefit to all sentient beings of the future.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi remained silent.
Knowing that he had consented, the king immediately arrayed his fourfold army to escort him from the front and rear;
he then returned to the palace together with the Bodhisattva, riding in the same carriage.
They also prepared parasols, banners, streamers, incense, flowers, music, and performances as offerings to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, there was a royal city named Uttara;
when the people within the city heard that the Bodhisattva was coming, they [prepared for his arrival].
Along the path he traveled, people vied with one another to offer him incense and flowers as worship.
Once the Bodhisattva had arrived at the palace,
Jingjinshou (Vīryadatta) further prepared for him lion thrones made of the seven precious gems.
Please invite the Bodhisattva to his seat and present various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels;
offer jeweled vases filled with the most excellent *argha* perfumed water;
and present the fivefold offerings to the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there was a great multitude of bhikṣus who,
desiring to hear the Dharma, also brought fragrant flowers to offer to the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi...
Then, according to the ritual procedures heard from the Buddha,
he entered the great maṇḍala and conferred the consecration upon the king with vajra-purifying water.
After Vīryadatta had received the empowerment,
there were also assemblies of bhikṣus, as well as kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and others,
all of whom came to the royal palace to the place where the Bodhisattva was.
Desiring to hear the Dharma,
he gave rise to the bodhicitta and entered the Vajrayāna.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi...
He then proceeded to explain for him the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
as well as the characteristics of the various faculties and dharmas,
and the methods of nidāna and so forth.
This extends even to the Tathāgata family, the Vajra family, the Ratna family, the Padma family, and the Karma family,
according to the correspondences of the Vajrayāna and through the skillful means of samādhi, samāpatti, and so forth.
He caused them all to attain liberation and reach the ultimate realm of nirvana.
At that time, there was a king of South India named Vīradatta,
who possessed profound faith and deep reverence.
They joyfully seek the supreme Dharma and enter the Vajra Mahāyāna;
furthermore, they joyfully seek the samādhis and samāpattis that accord with the dispositions and faculties of sentient beings.
Having mastered skillful means, he attained the patience of non-arising and reached the limit of the realm of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there was a king of Northern India named Viryavarma who did likewise.
The King of East India, named Subāhu, was likewise so;
the King of West India, named Śatabāhu, was likewise so.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus.
Carrying various precious and exquisite garments,
they came simultaneously to where the Bodhisattva was,
making offerings, paying respect, prostrating, and circumambulating him.
They addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"With our profound resolve, we joyfully seek the supreme Vajra Mahāyāna;
we likewise joyfully seek the samādhis and samāpattis that correspond to the natures of sentient beings."
Having mastered all skillful means, they realize the patience of non-arising and exhaust the realm of nirvana.
At that time, there were also among the populace of the land those who saw, heard, and rejoiced in this.
They all likewise gave rise to the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*).
At that time, there were also many Vajrācāryas in the world, namely:
Jñānāśva, Jñānadatta, Dharmāśva, Bhadradatta, Guṇadatta, and Sāgaradatta.
These and other ācāryas,
having heard the corresponding Dharma taught by the Bodhisattva,
all fully realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the King of Eastern India, Subāhu,
together with the ladies of the inner palace— the queens, concubines, and court attendants—
as well as the citizens of the city and the assembly of those who delight in the Dharma, [all gathered].
Furthermore, within the fundamental and supreme Dharma, through the practice of samādhi,
one attains the accomplishment of mastery over invisibility.
Moreover, there were various Vajrācāryas in India who [possessed this].
These were known as Bhadrasena, Guṇasena, Śāntisena, Udrasena, Anantagarbha, Devagarbha, Balagarbha, and others.
There were also various brāhmaṇas.
Namely, the Nāta brāhmaṇas, the Harisvāmin brāhmaṇas, the Bhāṇḍilika brāhmaṇas, and the Padma brāhmaṇas.
In this manner, these ācāryas, brahmins,
and others heard the Vajra Mahāyāna taught by the Bodhisattva,
as well as the methods for the corresponding samādhis.
They all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, King Śatadru (Hundred-Armed) of Western India,
along with those in his inner palace— the queens, concubines, and court ladies— [all attained it as well].
Having heard the profound Vajra Mahāyāna and the essential points of all dharmas as taught by the Bodhisattva,
they have all fully realized the methods for accomplishing the samādhi that is encompassed by and corresponds to vajra-wisdom.
And [he attained] mastery over concealment.
Furthermore, within that land of India, there were many Vajrācāryas, namely:
Jñānaguhyaka, Kalyāṇaguhyaka, Bhadraguhyaka, Prajñāguhyaka, Prajñābhadra, Vimalabhadra, and others.
There are also various Vaiśyas,
namely: the Vaiśya Sumati, the Vaiśya Indrarāja,
the Vaiśya Indrarāva, the Vaiśya Vimalaprabha, and so forth.
These ācāryas, viśas, and others,
having heard the supreme Vajra Mahāyāna and various sublime dharmas spoken by the Bodhisattva,
all fully realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
The King of Northern India, Viryavarma,
together with the ladies of the inner palace, court ladies,
and the common people, including śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Those who delight in entering the Vajra Mahāyāna shall,
within this Dharma, hear the essential points of the teaching expounded by the Bodhisattva;
they shall also attain the accomplishment of the samādhi of true correspondence subsumed within vajra-wisdom, as well as mastery over invisibility.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
for the sake of those kings, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and even vaiśyas,
expounded the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna and the essential points of all dharmas over the course of six years.
May those kings and the assemblies who delight in the Dharma all obtain benefit and happiness.
Furthermore, he shall expound upon the various methods of accomplishment,
namely the eight great sacred medicines.
The eye-salve, sword, and noose;
the vajra-wheel and vajra-pestle;
the precious vase, leather sandals, and so forth.
And the caves of humans and asuras,
up to the various methods for achieving love and devotion;
at that time, all kings, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others [were present].
They constantly followed him to listen to and receive his instructions.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva addressed the assembly, saying:
"In that region there is a great mountain named Mahendra."
The summit of that mountain is level,
upright, and vast. There are also gardens, groves, ponds, and pools—
places of delight— for you all, O kings, as well as for śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and others.
"All those who practice and study the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna may go together to that mountain to practice and dwell there.
Later, at another time, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying:
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Pure Radiance of that day is about to enter nirvāṇa.
You should now come with me to the Buddha’s presence to request and receive empowerment.
At that time, the assembly of practitioners of the Vajra Mahāyāna,
together with the bodhisattvas, took various kinds of exquisite incense and flowers and proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata Sun-Pure-Light resided.
Having arrived there, he presented incense and flowers,
performed a great offering, circumambulated [the Buddha] while praising him,
and prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet.
Having completed their acts of veneration, they sat together before the Buddha.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, in the presence of the assembled multitude,
bared his right shoulder and placed his right knee upon the ground.
Placing his vajra-palms upon his own heart,
he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "I shall follow the Tathāgata’s instructions and go to that royal palace for the sake of the kings, as well as the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
Furthermore, for all those who have resolved to attain enlightenment and seek to study the Vajra Mahāyāna, he expounds the Vajra Mahāyāna,
as well as the various dharmas pertaining to the faculties, their objects, their focal points, and their activities.
May they all attain the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
World-Honored One, I now wish to receive empowerment within the Tathāgata’s Vajra Mahāyāna teachings,
together with this assembly of students.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant his permission.
At that time, the Tathāgata Sun-Pure Radiance looked around to his left and right.
Immediately, he emitted a great radiance from his mouth;
in a single kṣaṇa, that light of five colors illuminated Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
It shone forth, illuminating everything up to the Brahma world;
having thus illuminated them, it immediately returned and re-entered through the World-Honored One’s mouth.
At that time, all the Tathāgatas of the Buddha-fields illuminated by that light of radiance praised him in unison, saying:
"That Vajra Mahāyāna subsumes all vehicles."
This applies likewise to the past, future, and present.
That Vajra Mahāyāna subsumes all vehicles;
at that time, the assembly of disciples all received empowerment within the Vajra Mahāyāna.
Having received the empowerment,
they all prostrated with their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Sun-Pure Radiance (Sūryaviśuddhaprabha), and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
They then circumambulated them a thousand times, joyfully offered praises, and each returned to their original place.
At that time, not long thereafter, the Tathāgata Sun-Pure Radiance entered parinirvāṇa.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma remained for a thousand years.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva again went to Mount Mahendra and dwelt there.
Then, all the members of the Mahāyāna Vajra assembly addressed one another, saying:
"Our original teacher, the Bodhisattva, has returned to that mountain.
We ought to go together to that mountain to serve and make offerings to him,
and to personally practice all the activities of the Vajra Mahāyāna."
At that time, the entire assembly of disciples, including all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
each taking incense, flowers, and various ritual offerings,
went together to the presence of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva on Mount Mahendra.
Having reached that mountain, they each presented incense, flowers, and precious playthings as offerings to the Bodhisattva;
they circumambulated him, prostrated, and remained there gazing up at him.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva beheld that assembly of students.
They all came to the mountains to attend upon and make offerings to him;
they cultivated their practices with firm resolve.
He then addressed the assembly, saying: "Each of you..."
Having heard the essential teachings on all phenomena from me, the Supreme Vajra Mahāyāna,
you shall all realize the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and exhaust the realm of nirvāṇa. Listen attentively!
"My teacher, the Tathāgata Sun-Pure-Luminosity, has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Sentient beings have meager merit and no one to rely upon.
What I have told you, you must practice well."
After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, that Vajrācārya shall be your teacher.

Why is this? Because that ācārya is able to protect and uphold the buddha-field, and because he is able to protect and uphold the secret vajra-dharma, he is capable of proclaiming the four-syllable name.
This is precisely the mark of a Tathāgata.
You, the great assembly, should always show respect,
prostrate, and make offerings to that teacher, regarding him as identical to a Buddha.
Thereupon, one will immediately receive the constant protection and guardianship of all Tathāgatas;
it is as if seeing all the Tathāgatas before one's eyes.
You, members of the assembly of students, should always serve and provide for that teacher.
Regarding all items for his use— seats, bedding, clothing, medicinal decoctions,
and everything else required— one must ensure that nothing is lacking; yet,
although one constantly attends upon him, one must not allow one's feet to tread upon the teacher’s shadow.
All fellow students, regardless of whether they are close or distant,
should regard one another with a single mind of equanimity. Good son,
if there are practitioners or any other persons who [disrespect] the Vajrācārya and the various students of the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna, [they shall incur great fault].
Having conceived a lack of faith and given rise to evil thoughts, they further proceed to slander [it].
The retribution for such a person shall be falling into the hells, the animal realm, and other evil destinies.
Why is this? Because all dharmas arise from that [source].
If there are those who disparage it, they are in fact disparaging the Dharma, and therefore receive this retribution.
If there are sentient beings who have not yet severed the cycle of saṃsāra and come seeking instruction,
one should expound the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna for them according to their individual capacities.
"May they be caused to enter the Vajra Samādhi.
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva further declared:
"This Vajra Mahāyāna is indeed all the Tathāgatas."
All Tathāgatas are themselves Great Wisdom. If any among you,
the assembly of students, do not rely upon samādhi and violate my teachings,
I shall cause you to be destroyed like ashes.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva gave the Vajra-water for the students and others to drink.
He then formed the Great Wrathful Mudrā and placed it upon the crowns of the students' heads;
having thus performed the empowerment, he concluded.
Furthermore, he addressed them again, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, this body of yours is now sustained by the Vajra-samādhi.
Should anyone commit a transgression or fail to comply with it,"

By means of my Vajrasamādhi-mudrā and the Wrathful Mudrā, I shall cause them to be destroyed; furthermore, the Bodhisattva shall, according to the ritual procedures of the former Buddhas, bestow the empowerment upon the assembly of disciples.
Furthermore, he recites the Awakening Mantra to cause them to awaken.
He then shows them the vajra, causes them to state their own names,
and bestows empowerment upon the eight parts of the bodies of his disciples.
At that time, the assembly of Vajrayāna Mahāyāna practitioners,
having completed all the rules of training received from the Bodhisattva,
immediately turned toward the Bodhisattva.
Having praised, honored, and made offerings to that bodhisattva in various ways,
they addressed him again, saying: "Each of us shall act according to the bodhisattva’s instructions before the Vajrācārya."
They served, made offerings to, revered, and praised him exactly according to his holy instructions.
At that time, having completed his transformative activities, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi vanished on the spot and was no longer seen.
The Supreme Mahāyāna Vajra Great Teaching Jewel King Sūtra, Volume One;
The Supreme Mahāyāna Vajra Great Teaching Jewel King Sūtra, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Great Master Dengyō, the Subject Fǎtiān, respectfully translated [this] by imperial decree.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Great King Indrabhūti, saying:
Great King, in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya great kalpas ago,
during the Dharma of the Tathāgata Sun-Pure-Radiance (Sūryaviśuddhaprabha),
you were already a king named Vigatotsāha (Vigorous Bestowal).
At that time, together with the assembly of students,
you already sought instruction from that Buddha regarding the Vajra Mahāyāna and the essential points of all dharmas.
Now, here in this Sahā world, in the presence of me, Śākyamuni Buddha—
Furthermore, when seeking to study such a Vajra Mahāyāna,
Indrabhūti, having heard these words,
immediately joined his palms and addressed the Bhagavān, saying:
"What is meant by 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva'? The Buddha said,
"If there is one who delights in practicing great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity,
this person is precisely what is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One looked toward his left and addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, saying:
"You should [act] just as in those past kalpas."
During the time of the Tathāgata Sūryavimalaprabha,
for the sake of the Great King Indrābhuji,
he taught the Vajra Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, he taught the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and various dharmas such as the faculties and their objects,
employing skillful means to bring about understanding and cause them to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder,
and having prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, paid him homage.
Placing his palms together at his heart, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "I shall now, in accordance with the Tathāgata’s instruction, expound [it]. Having heard these words, Indrabhūti [responded].
With the hairs on his body standing on end and his heart filled with great joy,
he rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One,
and then again prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
Having completed the rites, he addressed him, saying:
"I pray only that the Bodhisattva will honor the Buddha’s command,
go to my palace, and expound the teaching for me."
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, having received the Buddha’s command and observing that Indrabhūti’s mind and body were filled with earnest devotion,
silently granted his consent.
Indrabhūti, having silently given his consent,
prostrated at the feet of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; then,
leaping for joy, he paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
He immediately arrayed the fourfold army to lead and follow him from front and rear;
then, together with the Bodhisattva, he mounted a precious chariot,
spread out parasols and canopies, and played various kinds of music.
Having paid respectful homage, he returned to the great city of Puṇḍravardhana.
Along the path traversed by the Bodhisattva within that city,
all the people individually offered incense and flowers as an act of worship.
Having arrived at the palace,
Indrabhūti had previously prepared a great lion throne made of the seven precious gems; the Bodhisattva descended from his carriage and ascended that throne,
as did the king, the ladies of the inner court, the queen, and their retinue.
Furthermore, they arranged various kinds of incense, flowers, precious gems, and exquisite garments to perform a great offering.
They also presented to the Bodhisattva jeweled vases filled to the brim with *argha* perfumed water.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi [practiced] the samādhi and samāpatti of the vajra Great Vehicle secret correspondence, exactly as he had heard it from the Buddha.
He extensively expounded upon various dharmas,
desiring to cause the king and others to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and exhaust the realm of *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, there were also many śramaṇas, brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and others.

He also came to the royal palace desiring to hear the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna and various sublime teachings; furthermore, there was the Dharma-rāja King Prabhākara of the country of Malava in Eastern India.
King Ajita of North India; the Great King Candraprabha of West India;
and King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha.
King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī, King Brahmadatta of Licchavī,
and countless other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
as well as countless sentient beings who had resolved upon bodhicitta,
also came to the royal palace desiring to hear the Dharma.
In this way, these various people,
each with faith, reverence, and joy, came to the royal palace;
these various people, each with deep faith and joyful exultation, were filled with fervor.
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi said:
"We delight in entering the Vajra Mahāyāna and wish to hear various sublime teachings."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi,
for six years, expounded for the sake of the various kings and the multitudes of people the practices of the Bodhisattvas of the Vajra Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, he extensively expounded upon countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of samādhis and samāpattis that are in accord with reality,
as well as all dharmas pertaining to objects of perception, focal points, and activities.
At that time, because Indrabhūti had heard the Dharma,
he realized samādhi and samāpatti within the practices associated with all the Tathāgatas.
They attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and the realm of nirvāṇa,
as well as mastery over invisibility,
extending even to the ladies of the inner palace, the queen, their retinues, and the common people within the kingdom.
They heard the Vajra Mahāyāna and the essential points of all dharmas,
and all attained the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Furthermore, within that land, there was a Vajrācārya.
They are known as the virtuous dragon, the dragon of meaning, Jewel-Sound, Precept-Sound,
and Radiant-Sound. Furthermore, there were brahmins such as Dharma-Dragon, Power-Worthy, and others,
who attained [realization] within the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna teachings.
Having realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and exhausted the realm of nirvāṇa,
there was the Dharma-Glorious Great King of the country of Malava in Eastern India,
who [was established] within the most supreme Vajrayāna Mahāyāna teachings.
Having realized the supreme fundamental yoga-dharma,
he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), reached the limit of the realm of nirvāṇa,
and acquired mastery over invisibility.
Furthermore, from the ladies of the inner palace, consorts, and their retinues, down to the officials and commoners of the kingdom,

all who heard the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna and its various sublime teachings attained the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and reached the limit of nirvāṇa. Within India, there was moreover a Vajrācārya.
They were named the Tathāgatas Bhadradatta, Devadatta, and Suradeva.
Furthermore, there were Kṣatriyas such as Yaśovarmā, Maṇivarma, and Varma,
who likewise heard the Dharma within the Great Vehicle of the Vajra.
They all realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and reached the limit of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, there was King Aparājita of Northern India,
who heard the Vajra Mahāyāna and the essential points of all dharmas.
Thereupon, within the teachings of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*,
he realized the samādhi of correspondence, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), reached the limit of the realm of nirvāṇa,
and obtained mastery over the invisibility of his body.
Furthermore, there were also members of the inner court, including the empresses, consorts, and ladies-in-waiting, as well as commoners and gentry, who,
upon hearing all the sublime teachings of the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna,
fully realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
In that land of India, there was also a Vajrācārya named Bhadrapriya and Kamalapriya;
furthermore, there was a Kṣatriya named Unnatabrahma.
Furthermore, there was a Vaiśya named Dharmagupta.
Because these and other such assemblies had heard the Dharma within the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna,
they all realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and reached the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there was the Great King Candraprabha of Western India,
who, through hearing all dharmas from the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna,
realized the samādhi of the correspondence with the Vajra Speech and other attainments.
They attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and reached the limit of the realm of nirvāṇa;
they also attained mastery over invisibility.
Furthermore, there were those from the inner palace—the queens, concubines, and court ladies—down to the commoners and citizens.
Furthermore, there were Vajrācāryas named Amoghasiddhi, Viśvasiddhi, Tathāgatasiddhi, and so forth;
there were also Kṣatriyas.
Their names were Sumati and Suriyavarma.
Because these and others had heard the sublime Dharma from the Vajra Mahāyāna,
they all realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and reached the limit of nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi expounded for those kings and the entire assembly of students all the dharmas of the Vajra Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, he expounded the methods for accomplishing eight types of attainments:
namely, those of the sacred medicine, eye-salve, sandals,
sword, lasso, vajra-wheel, vajra-pestle, and the precious vase.
Furthermore, he expounded the methods for entering the stages (*bhūmi*) and the asura caves to achieve accomplishment.
He also expounded the conduct to be practiced by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas according to the Vajra Mahāyāna.
Regarding the various phenomena of the sense faculties, their objects, focal points, and activities,
he caused those disciples to each practice diligently and remain free from indolence.
During this time, for six years, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi...
For the sake of all kings and the entire assembly of students seeking the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna,
he expounded the various dharmas through diverse skillful means, parables,
and expressions, causing each of them to realize awakening.
He then addressed the assembly, saying:
"You should know that there is now a great mountain named Kikina at that place."
The summit of that mountain is level, vast, and expansive;
it also contains groves of trees, ponds, and pools—places of delightful serenity.
I shall go there first, while you all enter the assembly of all practitioners—the kings of the Vajra Mahāyāna, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and all those of learning.
One may also go together with them to that assembly.
At that time, once the assembly of disciples had all gathered at the summit of that mountain,
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva spoke again, saying:
"Now, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni is about to enter parinirvāṇa.
You all should now accompany me to the Buddha’s presence to request and receive empowerment.
At that time, the assembly of students immediately departed from that mountain together with Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva.
At that time, the various kings, leading the fourfold army as attendants before and behind,
and having prepared various great offerings, proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
At that moment, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni—
Having already arrived at the city of Kuśinagara,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi,
together with his assembly of disciples, reached the place where the Buddha was.
Having prepared a great offering and presented it to the World-Honored One,
they circumambulated him three times to the right, prostrated, and offered praise, then sat before the Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi rose from his seat.
Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee on the ground,
he joined his palms in the vajra-mudrā and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have received the Buddha’s command to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Within the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna teachings,
for the sake of the assembly of students, he explained the objects of the various sense faculties, their spheres of activity, their functions,
and the diverse phenomena; through these, each attained individual realization or achieved *samādhi* and *samāpatti*.
Some have attained the patience of the Dharma and reached the limit of the realm of nirvana;
some have attained mastery over the invisibility of their bodies.
World-Honored One, I have thus expounded the Dharma for the benefit of others.
Now they have come to where the Buddha is,
desiring to receive empowerment from the Tathāgata for the sake of that assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked around to his left and right.
Immediately, five-colored light was emitted from the crown of his head;
its brilliance shone forth so intensely that in a single kṣaṇa it illuminated Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, reaching upward as far as the Brahma world.
Having thus illuminated [the world], the light immediately returned and re-entered through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, wherever the light had shone throughout the ten directions, [all beings attained peace].
All Tathāgatas, with one voice, proclaimed in praise:
"The Vajra Mahāyāna subsumes all vehicles,
including all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
All have taught this Vajra Mahāyāna, which encompasses all vehicles.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately conferred the consecration with vajra-water upon the entire assembly of practitioners of the Vajra Mahāyāna.
Once the assembly of disciples had received the empowerment,
they all prostrated with their heads to the ground, paying homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and at the feet of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
Having completed their prostrations, they praised him with great joy and circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times before each returning to their own places.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One, what shall this True Dharma be called, and how should it be upheld?
The Buddha said, “Ānanda, as for this True Dharma now...”
"It is named 'The Supreme Jewel King of the Mahāyāna'; thus should it be upheld.
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, having spoken this sutra, [remained silent].
He then entered parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara.
Subsequently, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi returned to Mount Kikina.
There were also many bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who had come to the mountain together.
At that time, the assembly of Vajra-disciples said to one another,
"Our original teacher, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi— "
"Furthermore, there is Mount Kikina;
we ought also to go to that mountain to approach and make offerings.
Each member of this assembly of students should take various kinds of incense, flowers, and precious playthings, and together proceed to that mountain."
Having reached that mountain,
they each offered fragrant flowers as an offering, prostrated, circumambulated,
and respectfully praised [the Buddha], then sat down to one side.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having surveyed the assembly of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and others, addressed them once more, saying: "You members of the assembly, listen attentively."
Each of you has already attained realization within this Vajra Mahāyāna;
all of you are indeed possessors of the Vajra Mahāyāna Dharma.
You should know that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [you shall act as his successors].
The Vajrācārya is your teacher, just as he was in the past, immeasurable kalpas ago.
When the Tathāgata Sun-Pure-Light appeared in the world,
there was a king named Vigataraśmi in that Buddha-field of Great Sublime Fragrance.
At that time, I also spoke in this same manner regarding the ritual for serving the Vajrācārya;
now I shall likewise speak again regarding the ritual for the disciple’s service to the Vajrācārya.
There are eight modes of service.
Then Indrabhūti said to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"What are these eight modes of service called?"
Vajrapāṇi said: "First, one must not call the teacher by name;
second, one should always refer to oneself as the teacher's disciple."
Third, to carry the teacher’s shoes;
fourth, to sweep and sprinkle the floor of the quarters;
fifth, to arrange and set out the teacher’s bed and seat.
Sixth, prostrating with the five limbs;
seventh, not harming or encroaching upon the teacher;
eighth, receiving instructions with trust and faith.
These are called the eight methods by which a disciple serves a Vajrācārya.
That Ācārya examines the disciple through these eight matters,
observing them day after day, month after month, and as the months accumulate into years.
If that disciple does not contravene these eight matters but remains single-mindedly without regressing,
the ācārya may accept them as his disciples.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva spoke again, saying:
"For example, the various kinds of insects, moths, and flying moths in the world are all born from conditions;
having fallen into this miserable realm, by what means can they escape?"
It is also like sentient beings in the worldly cycle of saṃsāra.
How can one transform karma to attain the state beyond arising and ceasing,
if not through being received by a Vajrācārya who teaches various sublime dharmas?
"By what means can one eliminate all afflictions, realize quiescence, and attain non-retrogression? Great King,
that Vajrācārya must first observe the characteristics, status, and social rank of the disciples he intends to receive."
"Then you may be entrusted with the Dharma of the two truths.
The King asked, "What are called the two truths?
The Bodhisattva replied, "The first is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and the second is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)."
The King asked, "What is called ultimate truth?
The Bodhisattva replied, "It is what is known as internal emptiness, external emptiness,
internal-and-external emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness."
The emptiness of the great, the emptiness of the ultimate truth,
the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned,
the emptiness of the absolute, and the emptiness of the limitless.
The emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of the essential nature;
the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-existence;
the emptiness of non-entities, and the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
"Emptiness of self-characteristics and emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence—Great King, these eighteen kinds of emptiness are called the True Reality (*tattva*).
Great King, you further asked: 'What is meant by "reality" (*satya*)?'"
The Bodhisattva replied: "If one understands that these eighteen kinds of emptiness are neither permanent nor impermanent,
for this reason they are called truths."
Why is this? It is because one does not perceive internal emptiness, nor does one perceive external emptiness;
one does not perceive internal-and-external emptiness, nor does one perceive the emptiness of emptiness;
one does not perceive great emptiness, nor does one perceive the emptiness of the ultimate.
They do not perceive the emptiness of the conditioned, nor do they perceive the emptiness of the unconditioned.
They do not perceive the emptiness of the ultimate, nor do they perceive the emptiness of the limitless.
They do not perceive the emptiness of non-alteration, nor do they perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
One does not perceive the emptiness of all phenomena, nor does one perceive the emptiness of non-existence.
One does not perceive the emptiness of intrinsic nature, nor does one perceive the emptiness of specific characteristics.
One does not perceive the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, nor does one perceive the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
In such emptiness, one does not perceive dual characteristics;
it cannot be apprehended even in the middle;
it is neither arising nor ceasing.
Neither bound nor liberated;
neither moving nor abiding;
neither light nor darkness.
Neither real nor unreal;
neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa;
neither increasing nor decreasing.
I say that all such various things are detached from body, speech, and mind;
this is what is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Your Majesty further asked: "What is meant by conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?"
That is to say, when one employs the four immeasurable minds toward the fundamental characteristics of deportment—
the five aggregates, the four elements, the six sense bases, the five objects, walking, standing, and the three realms—
this is precisely what is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The King asked again, "What further is called the ultimate truth?
The Bodhisattva replied, "Those various forms and appearances are like magical illusions and like mirages."
Like the moon in water, like a bubble on the water;
like a reflection in a mirror, like a dream;
like lightning, like a city of the Gandharvas.
Up to and including rainbows and halos—
if one attains such a vision regarding the characteristics of form,
this is called the ultimate truth.
If one practices and accepts these dharmas without abandoning ascetic practice,
one can realize Buddhahood and attain all-knowledge.
Great King, this extends even to the meaning of six hundred million characters.
It is neither dual nor differentiated;
all Tathāgatas speak thus. You have already heard this entire teaching of the Wisdom-Vajra.
These are all called the ultimate truths.
Great King, if you cannot observe and understand these two truths as they truly are,
then even if you practice with single-minded devotion for immeasurable eons, [you will not attain liberation].
Their efforts will be wasted, and they will ultimately be unable to reach the further shore of great wisdom.
Yet these two truths are that to which all Tathāgatas take refuge;
they act as father and mother, and provide a dwelling of tranquility.
And for the sake of nirvāṇa, for the sake of the *avivartika* [stage],
for the sake of the perfectly and universally awakened realization of all samādhis,
and for the sake of the sublime Samādhi of the Universal Gate.
Thus, there are these various kinds of merits.
Great King, all those who study the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna must single-mindedly select disciples who are in accordance with the Dharma.
Only for such a person may one explain these two truths;
this Dharma of the two truths is difficult to hear,
being hard to hear even for those pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas.
How much more so for those of the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika). At that time, Indrabhūti,
together with the assembly of Vajrayāna Mahāyāna practitioners...
Having heard this teaching,
they all bowed their heads to the ground in gratitude to the Bodhisattva.
Then Indrabhūti again addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"What characteristics should a disciple selected for this purpose possess?
The Bodhisattva replied, "There are four kinds of disciples and five types of *pudgalas*."
The King said, "How should one speak of the four kinds of disciples? I now wish to hear this.
The Bodhisattva replied, "The first is the Buddha Vehicle; the second is the Initial Vehicle."
The third is the practice of the beginner bodhisattva; the fourth is the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
These are called the four characteristics of the disciples.
How are these characteristics to be distinguished?
The Bodhisattva replied: "They shall attain peace and security, neither slandering nor blindly believing.
They will clearly understand each of the mantras, mudrās, and signs, and realize the Buddha-vehicle.
What do you think? It is like a blind person who has been guided by another."
Because one attains liberation through the realization of the Buddha-vehicle,
the disciple first relies on the teacher to learn the single conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
First, by means of the corresponding dharma, one enters *samādhi*.
They have not yet attained a thorough understanding of the two teachings of Exoteric and Esoteric;
nor do they know the two truths or the twelve links of dependent origination;
nor do they know the Prajñāpāramitā.
"This is called the characteristic of a disciple’s initial cultivation.

The King asked, "What are the five kinds of *pudgalas* of a bodhisattva? The Bodhisattva replied, "They are what are called the *tāntra-pudgala*, [the *tanu-pudgala*, the *tanu-tanu-pudgala*, the *adhimātra-pudgala*, and the *adhimātrādhimātra-pudgala*]."
The *candala* person, the *padma* person, and the *pauṇḍarīka* person.
"Audapala-pudgala: those who are able to fully practice hearing, faith, precepts, and giving are *upāsakas*. The King asked:
'How are the names and characteristics of these Bodhisattvas to be distinguished?'"
The Bodhisattva said: "One who, although having heard all dharmas,
forgets them entirely after a short time—
this is called an *udghaṭitajña* (or *utpāṭaja*) person."
If, despite having heard the secret teachings,
one is unable to analyze and expound them for others,
it is like a merchant woman who hides a bright jewel within her garment and does not reveal it.
This is called the *paṇḍita* person.
Alternatively, having attained faith and a heart of great compassion, they understand the Dharma upon hearing it;
like a knotless bamboo, they receive, uphold, and penetrate it.
This is called the *padma-pudgala*. Whenever they hear the meaning of the Dharma, they invariably maintain the view of a self (*ātman*).
It is like striking a drum in empty space: there is only sound, but no substance.
Because one who holds the view of a self is unable to benefit others,
this is called a *caṇḍāla* person;
such is the fourth type of upāsaka.
Furthermore, they are able to seek all dharmas with single-minded devotion,
receiving and upholding them with faith while abiding in the Vajrayāna.
Moreover, their mental nature is fierce and sharp, and they are learned and maintain the precepts.
One who is able to relinquish everything and realize the truth,
and whose every teaching accords with the capacities of sentient beings, is called a *ratna-pudgala*.
This one upāsaka was constantly able to preach various dharmas to his disciples.
At that time, the Vajrācārya selected his disciples in this manner.
If one obtains a pure, distinguished, and Dharma-conforming disciple,
one may then transmit the secret Mahāyāna and all its supreme meanings;
one should cause them to practice so as to ensure that the lineage of the noble ones remains uninterrupted.
Indrabhūti asked again: "How does one distinguish the secret Mahāyāna?"
The Bodhisattva replied: "In those Yoga, Exoteric, and Esoteric teachings, there are twenty kinds of maṇḍalas, all of which are designated as the Secret Mahāyāna.
I shall now briefly explain the sequence of the consecration maṇḍala."
When that consecrated ācārya wishes to perform the rite of consecration,
he first personally binds the seal of purification (*śodhana-mudrā*), selects an excellent location,
and establishes the positions for the maṇḍala.
Afterward, having instructed the disciples to perform the purification (*parisodhana*),
the ācārya consecrates five-colored threads and five-colored powders,
stretches them across the ground to demarcate the boundary, and constructs the maṇḍala.
Having arranged the seats for the noble ones and further empowered the *argha* vases, and having established them in their respective positions,
one then invites the noble ones to take their seats according to their stations. Once they are seated,
one immediately presents incense, flowers, *argha*, and other offerings.
Nevertheless, one may lead the disciple into the maṇḍala and bestow the empowerment upon them.
Once the disciple has received the empowerment,
they should immediately offer various incenses, flowers, and precious jewels to the ācārya.
Disciple, from this point forward, you have entered the stage of consecration within the Vajra Mahāyāna.
You must deeply examine and reflect upon the actions of your own body, speech, and mind.
If you can thoroughly comprehend this, it is called the Five Lamps.
If one does not fully comprehend this, it shall be called the "Five Darknesses.
Furthermore, the sequence for arranging the fire-altar (agnimaṇḍala) and all the various materials to be employed therein [are as follows].
First, prepare the *bhrāmarī*, *sruva* ladle, and so forth,
as well as the *kuśa* grass for the seat and the fuel for the *homa*.
The fuel should consist of the moist branches of green trees, along with the five grains, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and other such substances.
Alternatively, one may perform *homa*.
First, kindle the sacrificial fire naturally and perform the *homa*.
One should observe the color, form, shape, sound, fragrance, and other qualities of the flames.
If auspicious signs are obtained, this dharma is accomplished;
if inauspicious, it is not accomplished.
This refers to the invocation of the noble deities to enter the maṇḍala.
The procedures for the offering of argha and the sequence of rituals are for the most part identical.
All dharmas whatsoever flow forth from the Vajrayāna Mahāyāna Secret [Mantra].
All three yogas and five upapattigatis [are likewise derived therefrom].
Either the meaning of six *koṭi* of syllables,
or the meaning of the accomplishment of the Dharma,
or the definitive meaning.
Alternatively, it is taught as the *nidāna*, the *upāya*, the causes,
and so forth. These aforementioned [categories] may be fourfold,
fivefold, sevenfold, or twelvefold.
These various indeterminacies are all not apart from the two truths.
Furthermore, the four secrets are taught:
namely, the secret of the teaching, the secret of the meaning, the secret of the words, and the secret of the phrases.
If one achieves accomplishment through the four secrets without deviation,
then even when encountering the nine planetary deities, malevolent constellations, various poisons, and the like,
the recitation of the secret mantras can pacify them all completely.
Whether seeking to win over others through love, to perform rites of augmentation, or to perform rites of subjugation—
whether for humans, quadrupeds, multi-legged creatures, or those without legs;
or to subjugate various evil and great classes of yakṣas.
Even malevolent persons and the like can all be subdued.
If they are not subdued, they will surely bring about destruction, causing the separation of loved ones.
Or, all prohibitions, fetters, and malevolent mantras will be utterly destroyed.
Should enemies raise armies with the intent to inflict harm, they shall naturally disperse;
or in times of great drought, rain will surely fall.
In this manner, all various things sought shall be accomplished.
By reciting and maintaining these secret mantras, one shall achieve all accomplishments according to one's heart's desire.
Whenever reciting the mantras, one should employ the adamantine voice (*vajra-vāc*), ensuring there is no interruption;
thus, one’s aspirations will surely be fulfilled.
The King asked, "What is called the meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) of a bodhisattva?
The Bodhisattva replied, "Meditative concentration is of various kinds,
and the recitation of mantras is likewise of various kinds."
If one knows the secret phrases, one knows meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
"Secret" refers to the complete recitation of the textual passages and the knowledge of the mudrās.
If one acts in this manner, there will be great power.
This is the white dharma (*śukladharma*).
One who knows the secret encompasses the true principle,
for its essence is as tranquil as space.
Understanding worldly phenomena, one is able to manifest the ultimate truth;
thus, one contemplates the seals (*mudrā*) and resolves doubts regarding the meaning of the words and phrases of the secret mantras (*mantra*).
This practitioner of recitation is called "the virtuous.
Any who behold such a practitioner are as if beholding the Buddha himself.
That meditator does not perceive secret syllables.
One does not perceive the marks of seals, nor does one perceive noble beings.
One contemplates that the essence of all the wheels of syllables is identical to a reflection in a mirror.
The King asked again: "What is the samādhi of a bodhisattva?"
The Bodhisattva said: "That bodhicitta, as well as wisdom and skillful means,
up to and including the three types of higher knowledge and the unequaled—
these are all the samādhis of a bodhisattva."
Furthermore, one contemplates one's own body, as well as the forms of the mantras and mudrās,
and all the ornaments of the images of the worthy and holy ones,
as being entirely like empty space and quiescent.
This is the samādhi of the bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva enters such a samādhi,
it is called abiding in the two truths.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi [addressed] Indrabhūti and all the kṣatriyas,
as well as the entire assembly of those training in the Vajra Mahāyāna.
Having thus expounded these various teachings,
he constructed a maṇḍala according to the ritual rules and conferred empowerment upon the king, his retinue, and the assembly of students.
Once those disciples had received the empowerment,
they spoke with one voice, each addressing the Bodhisattva:
"We shall receive the instructions and serve the Vajrācārya exactly according to your holy command."
Having thus paid homage and respect to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi with various words of praise and gratitude,
the great bodhisattvas in the assembly at that time—
And when the śrāvakas, devas, humans, asuras, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and the entire great assembly had heard this sūtra spoken by the Bodhisattva, they were [filled with joy].
Rejoicing and receiving it with faith, they paid homage and withdrew.
Then, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva vanished from the mountain and became invisible.
